title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)

In this analysis, I look at median gross rent across counties in California and compare how reliable the estimates are. I use the margin of error to identify which counties have more or less uncertainty in their rent estimates.

vars <- load_variables(2023, "acs5")
View(vars)

my_state <- "CA"       
my_variable <- "B25064_001"    

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)


dim(county_data)

[1] 58  5

head(county_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  GEOID NAME                         variable   estimate   moe
  <chr> <chr>                        <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
1 06001 Alameda County, California   B25064_001     2318    17
2 06003 Alpine County, California    B25064_001       NA    NA
3 06005 Amador County, California    B25064_001     1380   106
4 06007 Butte County, California     B25064_001     1369    31
5 06009 Calaveras County, California B25064_001     1615   142
6 06011 Colusa County, California    B25064_001     1139    67


The state of California has 58 counties, and the row count was also 58.


county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)


county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                         estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                           <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Sierra County, California        1181   705   59.7 
 2 Trinity County, California        922   220   23.9 
 3 Plumas County, California        1034   148   14.3 
 4 Mono County, California          1593   212   13.3 
 5 Mariposa County, California      1268   165   13.0 
 6 Calaveras County, California     1615   142    8.79
 7 Modoc County, California          818    71    8.68
 8 Lake County, California          1292   110    8.51
 9 Tuolumne County, California      1247   103    8.26
10 Inyo County, California          1140    88    7.72


Sierra County had the largest margin of error relative to the estimate, with a margin of error percentage of 59.7%.

Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence    39
2 Low confidence      6
3 Moderate           13


[How many counties fall into each category?] From the total 58 counties in California, 39 counties were classified as high confidence, 13 as moderate confidence, and 6 as low confidence. —

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 06001 Alameda County, California     2318     17 1651949    NA
2 06003 Alpine County, California        NA     NA    1695   234
3 06005 Amador County, California      1380    106   41029    NA
4 06007 Butte County, California       1369     31  209470    NA
5 06009 Calaveras County, California   1615    142   45995    NA
6 06011 Colusa County, California      1139     67   21895    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))


county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         39        989118.
2 Low confidence           6         11691.
3 Moderate                13         45926.


** [What is the average population of high-confidence counties versus low-confidence counties? Is there a pattern?]**
The average population of high confidence counties is 989,117.82, and the average population of low confidence is 11,691.33. The pattern shows that less reliable estimates tend to occur in counties that have smaller populations.

We know the least about the smaller counties in California. Sierra County had a highest margin of error relative to its median gross rent estimate at 59.7%, and other smaller counties, like Trinity County, Plumas County, Mariposa County, and Mono County, had very high margins of error. These six counties, which were classified as low confidence had an average county population of 11,691.
Since the ACS only uses a sample of households rather than surveying every household in the country, there is less samples and therefore more uncertainty and larger margins of error when collecting data. The smaller counties having less reliable median gross rent estimates is explained by this.
This uncertainty plays a part in a situation where housing funding may be allocated based on an equally certain approach from a state agency. The high margins of error means that these smaller communities may be subjected to either too much money or too little money. Since the government has limited funding, a county receiving too much money can be detrimental to other counties who may need it. This ties into a county receiving too little money, because since their margin of error is not accounted for, the misallocation of funds further spirals.

The high margins of error means that these smaller communities may be subjected to either too much money or too little money. Since the government has limited funding, a county receiving too much money can be detrimental to other counties who may need it. This ties into a county receiving too little money, because since their margin of error is not accounted for, the misallocation of funds further spirals.

title: Verify the Claim: Inequality in Philadelphia
text: The provided article examined changes in poverty and inequality across Philadelphia using the American Community Survey (ACS). It compared the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 ACS 5-year estimated and reported large changes in poverty rates across several Philadelphia neighborhoods. For example, the article reported that Eastwick’s poverty rate increased from 12% to 26%, while Holmesburg’s poverty rate increased from 2% to 19%. Because the article’s neighborhood boundaries are not Census geographies and the tracts used to construct them are not provided, this analysis uses census tracts to evaluate the broader pattern of poverty rate change across Philadelphia rather than attempting to reproduce the article’s exact neighborhood estimates. I used ACS table B17001, with B17001_001 representing the population for the census tract and B17001_002 representing the population below the poverty level. I calculated the poverty rate as the population below as poverty divided by the population for whom poverty status is determined. I used the ACS 5-year estimates for 2010 and 2017, corresponding to the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 periods compared in the article. The article confirms that its latest data are from the 2013–2017 five-year survey and that comparisons are made with 2006–2010. These periods do not overlap, the first ends in 2010 and the second begins in 2013, so they share no survey years. My main assumption is that changes at tract level can be used to evaluate the article’s broad claims about geographic patterns of poverty change, but not its exact neighborhood level estimates.

title: Verify the Claim: Inequality in Philadelphia
text:
Part 2 — Test

Poverty Rates and Margins of Error
For each census tract, I calculated the poverty rate by dividing the population below the poverty level by the population for whom poverty status was determined. Sunce the poverty rate is a proportion rather than a count, I used moe_prop() to calculate its margin of error. This accounts for the sampling uncertainty in both the numerator and denominator rather than treating the ACS point estimate as an exact value.


Show code
phila_poverty_2010 <-phila_poverty_2010 %>% 
  filter(total_popE > 0) %>% 
  mutate( poverty_rate_2010= povertyE / total_popE, 
          poverty_rate_2010_moe = moe_prop(
            povertyE,
            total_popE,
            povertyM,
            total_popM ) ) 
  
phila_poverty_2017<- phila_poverty_2017 %>% 
  filter(total_popE > 0) %>% 
  mutate( poverty_rate_2017= povertyE / total_popE,
          poverty_rate_2017_moe = moe_prop( 
            povertyE, 
            total_popE,
            povertyM,
            total_popM 
       ) 
  )




Reliability
I evaluated the reliability of each poverty rate estimate using the CV (coefficient of variance). I first converted the 90% margin of error to a standard error by dividing by 1.645, then calculated the CV by dividing the standard error by the poverty rate estimate and multiplying by 100. Following the thresholds set by Jurjevich et al. (2018) , estimates with a CV below 12% were classified as reliable, estimates from 12% to 40% as somewhat reliable, and estimates above 40% as unreliable.


Show code
phila_poverty_2010 <- phila_poverty_2010 %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_se_2010 = poverty_rate_2010_moe / 1.645, 
    cv_2010 = (poverty_se_2010 / poverty_rate_2010) * 100,
    reliability_2010 = case_when(
      cv_2010 < 12 ~ "Reliable", 
      cv_2010 <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable", 
      TRUE ~ "Unreliable" 
      ) 
    )

phila_poverty_2017 <- phila_poverty_2017 %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_se_2017 = poverty_rate_2017_moe / 1.645, 
    cv_2017 = (poverty_se_2017 / poverty_rate_2017) * 100, 
    reliability_2017 = case_when( 
      cv_2017 < 12 ~ "Reliable",
      cv_2017 <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE ~ "Unreliable" 
      )
    ) 




Comparing the 2 Periods
I joined the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 estimates using the census tracts’ GEOID. I calculated the change in poverty rate by subtracting the 2006–2010 rate from the 2013–2017 rate. Positive values are representing the estimated increases in poverty, while negative values are representing estimated decreases.


Show code
phila_poverty_change <- phila_poverty_2017 %>% 
  left_join(
    phila_poverty_2010 %>% 
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    select(
      GEOID, 
      poverty_rate_2010, 
      poverty_rate_2010_moe, 
      poverty_se_2010, 
      cv_2010,
      reliability_2010 ),
    by = "GEOID" 
  )

phila_poverty_change <-phila_poverty_change %>%
  mutate( poverty_change = poverty_rate_2017 - poverty_rate_2010 )




Missing Values
I checked the tract level dataset for missing poverty rates and changes. No missing values remained among the tracts included in the comparison. Tracts where the population for which poverty status was determined was zero were excluded before calculating poverty rates because a poverty rate cannot be calculated with a denominator of zero.

  filter(
    is.na(poverty_rate_2010) |
    is.na(poverty_rate_2017) |
    is.na(poverty_change)
  )

Testing Change
To determine whether the change in poverty rate for each tract was distinguishable from zero, I combined the standard errors from the two periods and calculated the margin of error for the change. I then calculated a z score for each tract. At the 90% confidence level, a change was considered statistically detectable if the absolute value of its z score was greater than 1.645.


Show code
phila_poverty_change <- phila_poverty_change %>% mutate( se_diff = sqrt(poverty_se_2010^2 + poverty_se_2017^2), moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645, z = poverty_change / se_diff, significant = abs(z) > 1.645 )

Of the 376 census tracts included in the comparison, 63 had statistically detectable changes in poverty rate, while 313 did not. This does not mean that poverty did not change in the other 313 tracts, it just means their estimated changes could not be distinguished from sampling uncertainty at the 90% confidence level.


Statistically Detectable Changes


Show code
phila_poverty_change %>%
  filter(significant) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(poverty_change))) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  mutate(NAME = str_remove(NAME, " Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, poverty_change), y = poverty_change)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = poverty_change > 0)) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(
      ymin = poverty_change - moe_diff,
      ymax = poverty_change + moe_diff
    ),
    width = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Largest statistically detectable changes in poverty rate",
    subtitle = "15 census tracts, 2006–2010 vs. 2013–2017",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Change in poverty rate"
  )









The figure shows census tracts with statistically detectable changes in poverty rate and the margins of error surrounding those changes. The dashed line at zero represents no change. Values above zero indicate detectable increases in poverty rate, while values below zero indicate detectable decreases. The error bars show the uncertainty associated with each estimated change.

title: Verify the Claim: Inequality in Philadelphia
text:
Adjudication

Supported
The article’s broad claim that some parts of Philadelphia experienced substantial increases in poverty is supported by my analysis. The article describes “sharp increases in poverty in several neighborhoods” between 2006–2010 and 2013–2017. Of the 376 census tracts in my analysis, 63 had statistically detectable changes in poverty rates at the 90% confidence level. Of these, 36 were increases. This provides evidence that poverty increased in parts of Philadelphia during the periods examined.


Not supported
The data do not support interpreting poverty as having increased broadly across Philadelphia’s census tracts. Only 36 of 376 tracts had a statistically detectable increase, while 27 had a detectable decrease and 313 had changes that were not distinguishable from zero at the 90% confidence level. Therefore, the point estimates alone would overstate the evidence for change in many tracts. This does not directly contradict the article’s claim about particular neighborhoods, but it limits how broadly its description of increasing poverty can be applied.


Cannot be determined
The article specific neighborhood claims cannot be verified with my tract level analysis. For example, the article reports that Eastwick’s poverty rate increased from 12% to 26% and was the largest increase of any community, Fairhill had a 61% poverty rate, and Holmesburg increased from 2% to 19% in the article’s discussion of white poverty. The article does not provide the tract aggregation used to construct its neighborhood boundaries. In addition, my analysis measures overall poverty and does not test poverty by race or median household income. Therefore, the Holmesburg white poverty claim, the claim that poverty increased in 22 majority white neighborhoods, and the reported decline in Tioga-Nicetown’s median household income cannot be determined from this analysis.

title: Verify the Claim: Inequality in Philadelphia
text:
Rewriting the Article
New Census estimates show that poverty changed unevenly across Philadelphia between the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 ACS five-year periods. A tract level analysis found statistically detectable changes in 63 of 376 census tracts at the 90% confidence level. Of these tracts, 36 experienced increases in poverty rates and 27 experienced decreases. For the remaining 313 tracts, the estimated changes could not be distinguished from sampling uncertainty. Most poverty estimates were also classified as somewhat reliable based on their coefficients of variation, emphasizing the uncertainty present in ACS estimates. These results provide evidence that poverty increased substantially in some parts of Philadelphia, but they do not support interpreting the pattern as a uniform citywide increase. Specific neighborhood claims cannot be independently verified without knowing how census tracts were aggregated into the neighborhood boundaries used in the original analysis .
